p.t: Targets and minimum counts
Write at least 10 ideas yourself before using any AI tool, then expand the list with AI to 50 or more.
If fewer than 10 manual ideas exist, pause and brainstorm more before going on.
The 10-idea minimum gives the AI enough context and keeps its suggestions from being purely generic, without your market intuition.

Your manual brainstorm captures market intuition and unique angles, while AI finds systematic variations that meet your explicit criteria.

Brainstorm size matters before testing: reach at least 50 niche ideas on the worksheet.
Do not narrow down to one niche for the first store until the list holds at least 50 niche ideas.
Niche research should end with a list of at least 50 different niches that could be very profitable, from which the best are chosen to run.
The first module has one measurable goal: a list of 50 niche ideas, at least 10 of them personally brainstormed and the remaining 40 generated by AI.
The niche research step is complete only when the list reaches at least 50 niches. The task cannot be skipped, because the list is the foundation for scoring, validation and elimination.
Collect at least 50 niche ideas in the worksheet before moving on. Each idea is tested in the next research stage, which selects the best candidate for the first store.
A longer niche list gives more chances to find a winner, so add categories that could sell at higher prices and have not yet been considered.
Principles of the Brainstorm
The brainstorm only collects candidates; you do not need to be sure any idea is the best one. Profitability is checked later, where weak ideas are set aside.
Brainstorming produces candidates only, and every candidate must then be validated.
Brainstorm many ideas before choosing, because most will be weak and only one to three will fit you. Discarding weak ideas is a normal part of the process.
Generate ideas freely without filtering them against criteria during brainstorming, because filtering early kills ideas before they are developed. The goal of this stage is volume.
Add any idea that might work, even if it seems unlikely; strict filtering happens later in market research against defined criteria.
Sources differ on timing. One view says the research criteria must be set before brainstorming, because a list of a hundred niche ideas can still be all bad if you do not know what to look for.
The other says do not filter while generating; filtering comes after. Apply both: know your criteria first, and apply them only after the list is written.
Brainstorming is a habit. Opportunities for product ideas are everywhere once you look for them, and the idea list grows faster with practice.
Aim for a long idea list now, because the later action tasks ask for many ideas. Keep all ideas in one spreadsheet so they are ready for research.
Record product types rather than single brands or models, for example electric mountain bikes, car rims or chandeliers. Product types are broader and easier to research.
A market idea can be a product type or a market defined by its audience or interest. Both forms are valid, and you can use whichever is clearer to you.
A product-type idea names one specific item, such as a gear category like wetsuits or dive equipment.
An audience-type idea names the interest group and leaves the product range open, such as scuba divers who buy a range of diving gear.
Narrow a broad category, such as home furniture, into specific product types, such as sofas, dining room tables, patio furniture or hammocks, before researching niches.

Focus the brainstorm on physical products that cost more than $200. Earlier lessons set this threshold, and it applies to your own spending history too.
Review your personal purchase history and bank statements, noting products you have spent over $200 on.
These are established niches with proven demand from someone who understands the market firsthand.
People who make large purchases have validated niche demand with their own spending, so ask family and friends what they bought online for over $200.
Price is the only selection criterion at the first brainstorm stage: disregard personal passion and interests.

High-ticket examples: people who keep fish need aquariums and fish-keeping products that can sell for thousands of dollars, and coffee lovers buy high-end espresso machines priced from $1,000 to $6,000.
Avoid low-cost hobby lists, because cheap hobbies point to low-priced products, which does not fit a high-ticket model.
The model targets high-ticket items, so every source should be screened for products that could sell at high ticket prices.

Open the Source A X Research Worksheet in Google Drive or Excel.
Fill in Column A only on the Niche Research Worksheet tab.

**Worksheet procedure (keep in order)**
1. Open the Source A X Research Worksheet in Google Drive or Excel.

2. Add as many high-ticket niche ideas as come to mind, focusing on $200+ products.
3. Use simple observations from your home, office, gym or daily life for inspiration.

4. Fill in Column A only on the Niche Research Worksheet tab.
5. Mark this lesson complete.
6. Move to the next lesson to continue building your niche list.

**Build procedure (keep in order)**
1. Open the niche research worksheet in Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel or Apple Numbers. The app does not matter.

2. Fill the first column with the ideas from the earlier brainstorming.
3. Use the earlier brainstorming techniques first. They should reach 50 ideas on their own.

4. If the list is still under 50, add ideas from the resources below.
5. Do not filter yet. Collect candidates and leave testing for later.
Step 2: personal environment and purchase history
**Brainstorm order (keep in order)**
1. Look around your home and your workplace and write down physical products you see or own, keeping the $200 threshold in mind.
2. Open your credit card statements, find past purchases over $200, and add every physical product to your list.
3. Ask close friends and family which products they have bought, then ask a wider group, for example with a Facebook post to your connections.
Go through your hobbies: note products advertised in magazines and blogs, products mentioned or advertised in podcasts, product-type questions in Facebook groups about your hobbies, sidebar ads
and product reviews on blogs you follow.
5. Observe products in everyday places such as work, the gym, the shopping mall and the doctor's office, and add anything that could become a product idea.

6. Write every idea into column A of the niche research worksheet.
**Examples from everyday surroundings**
Everyday places are full of product ideas. At a doctor's office these include reception desks, medical chairs, examination lights, medical tools such as scalpels and lobby chairs.
At a gym they include weight machines and cardio machines.

Ideas can come from whatever is in front of you. Examples are a chandelier in your home, a built-in wine refrigerator in your kitchen, or car rims on a car next to you in traffic. Each goes straight onto the list.
A single living room contains more than 17 product categories that can be niches: chandeliers, wall lighting, table lamps, crown molding, wallpaper, coffee tables, sofas, fireplaces, mirrors, vases,
bookshelves, dining tables, dining chairs and wood flooring. Look around for product types.
Items to list from one living room photo include chandeliers, wall lighting, crown molding, lamps, sofas, coffee tables, wood flooring, dining tables and chairs, fireplaces, mirrors and bookshelves.
Product ideas can come from everyday observation, such as outdoor items, pools, fire pits, garden structures and large smokers seen around a home or on a walk.
Step 2: personal environment and purchase history (continued)
Niche ideas can come from everyday objects around you, such as furniture in your living room. Test each idea against the validation criteria before you commit to it.
Niche ideas can come from everyday observation, such as background products in movies or shows. Test each idea against the normal validation criteria before committing.

Everyday personal needs, such as children's play equipment, can suggest niche ideas that are worth checking against price and shipping criteria.
**Principles for personal sources**
Hobbies are a source of product inspiration, not a requirement. You do not have to build a business around a hobby you are passionate about to use it for niche ideas.
Record product types rather than single brands when you note an item from your surroundings.
Ask family and friends what products they have purchased online where they spent over $200,

Use this message as a direct message to people you know, or as a post to your own connections.
**Message template **
I'm researching which products would be viable to sell through online channels. Have you made any online purchases exceeding $200?
If so, I'd appreciate it if you'd share which specific products those were. Feel free to reach out if you'd like to know the reasoning behind my data collection-I'm happy to explain.
**Facebook and direct message template **
Hi, I am researching which physical products people buy online, and I would really appreciate your help.
If you have ever spent more than $200 while shopping online, could you send me a message with the names of the products you bought? Thank you in advance. P.S.
If you are curious what the information is for, send me a message and I will explain. Use this as a Facebook post to your own connections or as a direct message to people you know.
Replies usually name products people are willing to pay a lot for, which makes the post a good source for your niche list.
Step 4: hobbies, interests and magazines
**Hobby brainstorm procedure (keep in order)**
1. List things people do, love or are passionate about, such as hobbies, sports and interests, and not things they only have to do.
2. Use Google searches for lists of hobbies, activities and interests, and check books and specialist magazines for more ideas.

3. Write the ideas into a spreadsheet or on paper, aiming for about 20 ideas.
4. Do not evaluate them yet; the brainstorm is only the list that is researched next.

**Market-idea procedure (keep in order)**
1. Open the research tracker and work only in the Market Idea column.
2. Write down ideas without judging them against any criteria.
3. Each idea can be a product you could sell, a customer group you could serve, or an interest you could serve with products.
4. If you are stuck, take ideas from outside sources such as online searches, marketplace categories, magazines, library books, or hobby lists.

5. Keep adding ideas until you have at least 20 market ideas.
6. Only then move on to assessing the ideas against the other criteria.
**Interest-group procedure (keep in order)**
1. Brainstorm at least 20 market ideas, using paper or a spreadsheet, based on hobbies and interests you, your friends and family, Google hobby lists, and books or magazines.
2. For each interest group, list the high-ticket products its members would need or want to buy.

3. Run each idea through the six market criteria using Google Shopping and a keyword tool.
4. Mark each criterion yes, no or maybe in your tracker.

5. Prioritise ideas with yes on all six criteria; keep the others on the list in case they are needed.
**Google hobby-list procedure (keep in order)**

1. Search for 'list of hobbies' in Google.
2. Open one of the hobby lists that appear in the results.
3. Go through the listed hobbies one by one.
4. For each hobby, ask whether participants buy equipment or products, and if so, write that product or the hobby as a market idea.
Step 4: hobbies, interests and magazines (continued)

5. Move on to the next hobby until you have enough ideas.
**Hobby sources and examples**
Products that people buy for their own hobbies, see on special interest TV shows, or that friends and family use are good starting points.
People who already buy expensive products for a pastime are a strong signal for a high-ticket market.

Special interest magazines are useful because their advertisers are typically companies selling products for that interest. Flipping through a magazine's ads shows which product types are sold to that audience.
Ads in a hobby magazine or blog for a new type of product can be added to the list directly.
A mountain biker who sees ads for electric mountain bikes in biking magazines or forums would add electric mountain bikes as an idea.
One hobby list was described as containing 549 hand-picked hobby ideas, which gives a large pool to screen. This is one example of how a single search can deliver hundreds of candidate interests.
A Google search for a list of hobbies returns Wikipedia's list, a compiled list of about 549 hand-picked hobby ideas, and hobby category sites such as Discover a Hobby.
Together these give a large pool of candidate interests from a single search.
Hobby lists can be used from any country, because the hobbies are not tied to one region. A hobby that is popular locally but not in the target market should still be recorded and checked later.
Not every hobby contains products worth selling.
Hobbies that require equipment, supplies or specialised gear are promising, while hobbies that involve only giving advice or performing a skill often have no products to sell.
Beekeeping implies equipment purchases, and commercial t-shirt pressing may involve expensive machinery, so both are worth recording.
A handyman trade or giving advice typically has few products, so those are weaker candidates. Interior design usually involves many relatively high-priced home products.
An activity such as horse riding can be recorded as a market idea, or a specific expensive product linked to it, such as horse saddles, can be recorded instead.
Product ideas that look expensive can be written down now and researched later.
Step 4: hobbies, interests and magazines (continued)
On a Sports & Outdoors hobby page, bodybuilding, cardio workouts, cycling, golf, horse riding and camping are examples of hobbies that involve purchasable gear.
Each can be recorded as a market idea or narrowed to a specific product such as horse saddles.
Water hobbies such as kayaking and canoeing are worth recording because quality kayaks and canoes tend to be expensive. Water sports is a broader alternative label that can be used instead.
Crafts such as engraving and car detailing should be screened even though the craft itself is not a product. The tools and consumables used in these crafts can be the products to research.
A list of over 1,000 hobbies can be scanned for niche ideas. Not every hobby is a niche or a product category, so look for the ones that stand out.

Hobby-based expansion procedure:
1. Copy a hobby from the list.
2. If the hobby is unfamiliar, ask ChatGPT to define it first.
3. Paste the hobby into the prompt 'Please list examples of expensive products in the [niche] niche' or the equivalent wording.

4. Read the products and filter them using the same rules as for broad categories.
5. Add the remaining products to the niche worksheet.

Aquascaping, the craft of arranging aquatic plants, rocks and driftwood in an aquarium, produced these product ideas: rimless and Starfire glass tanks, ADA Solar Series lighting, Kessel freshwater LED lights,

aquarium filtration systems, CO2 systems and substrates.
**Hobby filters and sub-niches**
Passionate sub-niches such as travel can perform well on Facebook. Before entering one, check whether large players already dominate it and how big the market is.

**Pitch-a-niche (keep in order)**
1. Write down every niche you think is a good fit for dropshipping.
2. For each niche, write down the reasons behind your choice. The purpose is to bring out the underlying 'what for' motives that drive the choice.

**Timed first-reaction brainstorm (keep in order)**
1. Set a two-minute timer.
2. Write down as many possible niches as you can in that time.
3. Note the first thoughts that come up, such as worthiness, fear or excitement. These thoughts reveal the programming that will influence later decisions.

**Timing rule**
Complete the first brainstorm within 15-20 minutes.
Step 6: AI-Assisted expansion
**Expansion procedure (keep in order)**
1. Brainstorm and list at least 10 niche ideas manually on your niche research worksheet (10 is the minimum threshold; more is acceptable).

2. Open ChatGPT (free) or Gemini.
3. Copy the provided AI prompt for high-ticket niche expansion.
4. Paste the complete prompt into your AI tool.

5. Delete the placeholder line "paste your list here".
6. Return to your niche research worksheet.

7. Select all existing brainstormed niche ideas from your list.
8. Copy them.
9. Return to ChatGPT.

10. Under the section "Existing niches (Do not repeat):", paste your complete list.
11. Send the prompt to the AI and wait for results.

12. Click the copy icon to copy the full generated list.
13. Return to your research worksheet.

14. Position cursor in the row below your lowest existing niche number.
15. Paste the AI-generated ideas.

16. Delete any duplicate text that copied along with the niche names.
17. Delete extra rows to clean up formatting.

18. Resize columns to match your existing column widths and formatting.
19. Verify numbering is sequential and complete.

20. Mark the action task complete when finished.
**Shorter expansion procedure (keep in order)**
1. Open the Niche Research Worksheet (Google Drive or Excel) and confirm it contains at least 10 manually brainstormed niches.
2. Copy the AI prompt provided under this lesson and paste it into ChatGPT, Gemini, or your chosen AI tool.
3. Paste your existing niche list into the "Existing Niches, Do Not Repeat" section of the prompt, replacing the placeholder text.

4. Run the prompt in the AI tool and wait for it to generate 50+ new niche ideas.
5. Copy the AI-generated list.
6. Return to your worksheet and paste the new ideas into Column A, below your existing niches.
Step 6: AI-Assisted expansion (continued)

7. Remove any extra lines of copied prompt text and adjust formatting (row height, font) to match your existing list.
8. Verify your final niche list contains at least 50 ideas.

9. Mark this lesson complete and proceed to the niche check step.
**Rules for the AI step**
Paste your complete existing niche list into the "Existing Niches, Do Not Repeat" section of the AI prompt to prevent the tool from suggesting ideas you have already brainstormed.
Use the AI prompt to generate at least 50 additional niche ideas beyond your manual list. This quantity ensures a comprehensive pool of candidates to evaluate in market research.
Note the difference in counting: asks for at least 50 additional AI ideas beyond the manual list, while and count the final list as at least 50 with the AI supplying the remaining 40 goal.
Use whichever matches your plan, and make sure the final list reaches at least 50.
Expansion example: 17 manually brainstormed niche ideas plus the AI prompt generated 51 additional ideas that met all criteria, for a total research list of 68 niches qualified for supplier research
and demand validation.
Use ChatGPT (free tier available) or Gemini. Both tools process the same prompt structure and produce equivalent results for niche expansion.
Any AI chat tool such as ChatGPT or Gemini can suggest narrower sub-niches and higher-price variants of a broad niche. Its output is a list of ideas to test, not a verified demand source.
AI niche ideas must be checked against every research criterion before use, because the tool can return niches that break the rules, such as consumables or custom-only products.
ChatGPT draws on training data from a very large part of the internet, and for brainstorming it often produces ideas that a person would not reach through manual research alone.

Rug sub-niche prompt:
What types of rugs typically sell for $500 or more? Focus on rug types that appeal to upper middle class buyers, and leave out small area rugs that sell for less than $100 to $200.

List the rug categories and the materials they are made from.
**Filtering AI and expansion results**
Procedure for filtering ChatGPT results (keep in order):

1. Paste the broad category into the prompt and run it.
2. Read through the returned products.
3. Remove entries dominated by a few big brands, such as well-known skincare brands or luxury perfume houses.
4. Remove services, such as professional cosmetic procedures. Keep the products used to deliver those services, such as the equipment or supplies.
5. Turn single-brand items into generic product types. For example, change a specific brand of bike to fitness bikes or exercise bikes.

6. Keep plausible ideas such as home gym systems, high-end hair tools and home spa treatments.
7. Add the remaining items to the niche worksheet.

Some ChatGPT results are too advanced to start with, such as surgical robots. Advanced ideas such as advanced prosthetics can still be added at the brainstorming stage. They are checked later in research.
The expensive-products prompt on health and fitness returned high-end treadmills and ellipticals, branded exercise bikes, smart fitness tech, home gym systems and personal trainers.
Personal trainers are a service and are dropped, while generic items such as exercise bikes and home gym systems go on the list. Branded items are turned into product types before they are added.
Broad categories such as health, fitness and personal care are too wide to be a niche. Look for the specific sub-niche before adding a listing to the list.

If the listing gives no detail, the broad label should not be added as is.
Narrow broad categories into specific product types before testing them.
Sold stores, listings and marketplaces
**Business brokerage and sold-store research**
Business brokerage websites list online businesses for sale, showing asking price, business age and net profit. Browsing their online and technology section reveals which products real stores sell.
Use these sites for idea research only, not for buying a store.
The online and technology section of one brokerage site listed 1,368 businesses for sale at the time of recording.
A two-year-old Shopify store selling premium wall paneling was listed for almost $1.5 million and made about $600,000 net profit per year.
Premium wall paneling is therefore a niche to add to the list.
A current e-commerce listing for LED lighting was shown with $362,000 in sales per month. Listings for active stores with high monthly sales are useful for finding product categories.
Empire Flippers is a marketplace for selling online businesses, and its e-commerce section shows stores for sale with details.

Use the listings for research: look up what the store sells and which products it carries. A store listed for almost $3 million selling health, fitness, personal care and medical products is one example.
Sold-store and listing research can include content sites rather than pure e-commerce stores.
A content-driven site that sells gear still shows product categories, such as fishing, camping and hiking equipment, that are worth adding to the list.

**FE International procedure (keep in order)**
1. Open the section that shows businesses already sold.
2. Select the category e-commerce.

3. Note the names of the sold e-commerce companies.
4. Google each company name to see which products it sells.

5. Add the product types to the niche list. Not every sold store will be a winner.
**Marketplaces and category pages**
Wayfair.com is useful for browsing subcategories when brainstorming potential niches. Navigate its category structure to spark ideas for specific sub-niches within broader categories.
Brainstorm niche ideas from any source, including eBay's main collection page or Wayfair categories. Brainstorming only produces candidates, and each must then be validated.
For inspiration, look at Kickstarter for trending products with high prices, then search for other brands that make the same kind of product. This helps with brainstorming niches.

**Warnings for pre-made and public sources**
Do not start niche brainstorming by searching online for best dropshipping products or products to sell this year.
Those searches mostly surface middlemen suppliers and make it very hard to find something that works. Generate ideas from your own purchases, surroundings and daily life instead.
Ready-made lists of top-selling products or niches are shared with thousands of people, so the top items are usually too competitive. Do not start from such a list; generate your own market ideas.
Do not rely on pre-made lists of approved niches. When many people pick the same few markets, competition rises and those markets stop being profitable for everyone.
Find market ideas through your own research.
In dropshipping communities, asking other sellers for their winning niche is considered taboo. Generate niche candidates from your own research instead.
When brainstorming stalls, use outside sources to find ideas, such as internet searches on passions and hobbies,
marketplace category browsing, special interest magazines, library books, and hobby lists.
When a category produces a promising product, use that category name as a new search term in other sources, such as Google, magazines or libraries.

A single category can lead to a broader or more refined market idea.
Stuck-brainstorm procedure:

1. Go through a list of hobbies and mark the ideas that stand out.
2. Run each marked idea through the niche verification tool.
3. If an idea passes all checks, start building the store right away instead of delaying.

Note on the 2019 procedure: it moves straight to building the store once an idea passes its checks. Current guidance requires at least 50 niche ideas before narrowing to one niche for the first store.
Narrowing and filtering the list

**Quick checks (keep in order)**
1. Brainstorm a broad initial list of niches.
2. Filter the list using the quick checks: electronics, emotional attachment, strict deadlines, personalized items that must be seen or felt, and seasonality.

3. Verify the remaining niches against size, price and target demographic before committing.
**Connection, passion and market size**

Do not limit yourself to one niche at the start. If you have a personal connection to a niche, start there; otherwise choose by problem and market size. Sub-niches can be built later within the same problem area.
Pick a niche by listing the brands you would like to resemble and studying the customer base they already attract.
If your brand differs clearly from those brands, build your own audience instead of copying theirs.
Passion is set aside at the first brainstorm stage, where price is the only criterion.
Conflict: the first brainstorm disregards passion and interests, while the Source C approach starts from a personal connection when one exists.

Use the price-first list for the initial 50, and apply the personal-connection rule when choosing where to begin among the survivors.
**Other filters**
Hobbies that require equipment, supplies or specialised gear are promising; hobbies that only involve advice or skill are weak candidates.
Do not start with a single niche: scoring, validation and elimination happen.
Sources warn against starting from a short list of pre-approved niches, against broad labels, and against cheap hobbies.
A list of a hundred niche ideas can still be all bad if the research criteria are not set before brainstorming.
Avoid searching for best dropshipping products or products to sell this year at the brainstorm stage.
Do not request winning niches from other sellers; generate candidates from your own research.
